title: API Degradation Failure Modes & Rapid Fallbacks
summary: Compact reference for on-call engineers to quickly identify failure modes for API degradations (timeouts, 429s, streaming stalls, elevated 5xxs) and apply safe rapid fallbacks to preserve customer-facing availability while preserving signal for root-cause analysis.
quick_actions: Check global error rate and top 5 routes in past 5m
Verify recent deploys and rollout percentage
Toggle traffic to fallback model/region if available
Apply temporary rate-limiting policy or shed non-critical lanes
Open incident if customer-facing latency > SLO or > 3% error rate
body:
Purpose:
This draft captures a minimal set of actions for the first 30 minutes of an API degradation incident. The goal: reduce customer-visible impact quickly, avoid cascading failures, and preserve request/trace data needed for RCA. This is not exhaustive—use team SRE judgement for edge cases.

Scope and failure modes covered:
- Client-facing timeouts (requests hitting gateway/proxy/edge timeout thresholds)
- HTTP 429 rate limiting bursts (global or per-customer)
- Degraded streaming (token stalls, truncated streams, partial payloads)
- Elevated 5xx/503 rates from model backend or runtime

Observable symptoms (signals to watch):
- Latency P95/P99 spikes > baseline by 3x
- Error budget burn: error-rate > SLO threshold for >5 minutes
- Spike in 429s from API gateway or from internal rate limiter logs
- Long tail of open connections / large number of connections in TIME_WAIT on workers (indicative of backpressure)
- Streaming sessions reporting last-ack but no further tokens

Initial triage (0–5 minutes):
1) Confirm incident: check primary dashboards (Console -> per-route latency and error rate).
2) Scope: identify affected routes, models, regions, and client keys. Narrow to smallest blast radius.
3) Rollback/deploy check: query the deployment service for recent rollouts (last 30m). If a rollout is ongoing, pause/rollback to last stable image.
   - Command example: kubectl -n runway get rollout my-runtime -o yaml (or check our internal rollout UI)
4) Preserve signal: increase sampling for traces and request dumps for the affected routes. Do not globally increase sampling for all traffic for extended periods.

Rapid mitigations (5–20 minutes):
A. Timeouts and latency spikes:
  - Short-term: reduce per-request complexity (lower max tokens, shorter truncation) by applying a route-level override to template defaults. Switch to a smaller model variant (e.g., gpt-lite-7b) if semantics allow.
  - If the issue is worker queue saturation: temporarily increase worker pool in the affected region by adding GPU nodes to the pool or enabling burst nodes. Use autoscaling override rather than full cluster change where possible.
  - Apply circuit-breaker: reject requests that exceed known heavy patterns (large batch sizes, long sequences) with friendly 4xx and guidance to retry with smaller payloads.

B. 429s (rate limit saturation):
  - Determine source: gateway-level 429 vs. backend-generated 429. Check gateway logs (nginx/edge) and internal limiter metrics.
  - If gateway-level: consider relaxing global rate limit thresholds for a short window or increasing token bucket refill for high-tier customers. Prefer granular increases over global.
  - If backend-level (model backend returning 429 due to queue/backpressure): route low-priority customers to degraded path or cached responses, enable greedy-fallback to a cheaper cached embedding/generation, or scale up capacity.
  - Temporary policy: enable token-based priority for enterprise keys to preserve SLAs while shedding free-tier burst traffic.

C. Degraded streaming (stalling or truncated events):
  - Check keeper metrics: streaming-ack timestamp deltas, open-connection counts, last-token timestamps per session.
  - If only a subset of streaming workers are affected, mark them as drained and shift new streaming sessions to healthy workers.
  - If edge is dropping frames due to slow downstream: reduce streaming chunk size and increase idle keepalive, or fallback to non-streaming responses for new sessions.
  - If the model runtime crashes mid-stream, return an explicit error to client and mark the request for replay in the debug queue.

D. Elevated 5xx rates from runtime/model:
  - Identify whether errors are consistent (same exception) or diverse. Query logs for error signatures.
  - If a recent model binary or kernel change exists, rollback to previous runtime image.
  - If memory pressure / OOMs occurring: reduce concurrency per model instance (max_concurrency), reduce batch sizes, and restart affected pods gracefully to reclaim memory.

Safe fallback patterns (examples to apply quickly):
- Model variant fallback: route 100% of traffic for affected route -> a smaller, compatible model. Use feature flag gated fallback to avoid config drift.
- Regional failover: shift traffic from affected region to adjacent region with capacity. Use degradation mode to 80% of prior throughput and 20% error-tolerant bucket.
- Graceful degradation: prefer shorter responses, remove non-essential plugins (e.g., search re-rankers), and return cached answers for top queries.

Operational commands (examples for common actions):
- Check top error routes (PromQL): sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-gateway",status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (route)
- Check 429 source (gateway vs backend): sum(rate(http_requests_total{status="429"}[5m])) by (component)
- Drain a node: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- Scale up runtime pool quickly: our-infractl pool scale --pool runtime-eu-west --add 4 --reason "on-call emergency"

Escalation and communication (15–30 minutes):
- If mitigation does not restore customer SLO within 15 minutes, open an incident with severity SEV2 or SEV1 depending on customer impact. Populate incident doc with: start time, affected routes, mitigation steps, rollback decisions, and initial hypothesized root cause.
- Notify product and support channels with clear guidance (which customers may be impacted and any temporary workarounds).
- Assign an RCA owner and tag the incident with relevant labels for follow-up (deploy, capacity, runtime).

Post-incident checklist (RCA prep):
- Collect traces, request/response dumps, and core files from the timeframe.
- Capture autoscaling events and node provisioning logs.
- Record exact config changes (feature flags, rate limit overrides, rollout IDs).
- Run synthetic playback of failing requests against preserved staging snapshot.

Notes and operational pitfalls (lessons learned):
- Avoid long-lived global increases in trace sampling—high sampling can itself worsen latency.
- Prefer targeted fallbacks (route-level/model-level) rather than broad rollbacks which can hide signals.
- Feature flags must have a single source of truth and audit log; ad-hoc toggles across teams cause confusion during recovery.

Open questions / items to make more prescriptive before finalizing:
- Clear guidance on thresholds for automatic model fallback (P95 multiplier vs error rate)
- Standardized priority policy for shard-level 429s (how to allocate limited capacity across customers)
- Safe automated circuit-breaker behavior for streaming sessions

Appendix: example incident timeline (condensed)
- t=0: alerts for route /v1/chat P95 3x baseline and 4% errors.
- t=3m: verified a new rollout at 12% -> paused rollout, increased trace sampling for affected route.
- t=8m: applied model-variant fallback for /v1/chat to gpt-lite-7b; errors dropped to 0.8%.
- t=30m: opened RCA ticket; started post-incident data collection.
